source_text: μεῖς εἰς πονηρίαν, καὶ ἀσυμφανῆ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἔν γε δὴ σφίσιν αὐτοῖς τὴν τῶν ἠθῶν ἔχοντες μοχθηρίαν. Παραπέφυκε δὲ ἀεὶ τοῖς τὴν ἐπάρατον ἀλαζονείαν ἠῤῥωστηκόσι, τὸ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐθέλειν οὓς ἂν δύναιντο τυχὸν, καὶ πολυτρόποις κακουργίας ἐκπολιορκεῖν εὑρήμασιν, καθαρπάζειν δὲ οὕτω, καὶ τοῦτο ἀπλήστως. Ταύτῃτοι συνάπτει λέγων εὐθύ· «Καὶ στρουθὸν καὶ λάρον.» Ἀπληστότατα γὰρ οἶμαι ταυτὶ, καὶ τὸ παρεμπίπτον ἀεὶ συλλέγοντα. Εἶτά φησιν, ὅτι «Καὶ ἱέρακα καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ νυκτικόρακα, καὶ καταῤῥάκτην, καὶ ἴβιν, καὶ πορφυρίωνα, καὶ πελεκᾶνα, καὶ κύκνον.» Καταγράψειαν δ' ἂν ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς καὶ τόδε τοὺς ὠμῶς καὶ ἀγρίως ἐπιβουλεύοντας ἑτέροις, καὶ ἀσχέτως ἐπιφυομένους, οἷς ἂν δύναιντο τυχὸν, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸν ἐπιφέρειν οὐ παραιτεῖσθαί τισι τὸν ἐπὶ ζωῇ κίνδυνόν τε καὶ φόβον. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἱέραξ καταθρῶσκε· δεινῶς παντὸς ἀσθενεστέρου πτηνοῦ, καὶ κατὰ στρουθίων ἴεται, καὶ διόλλυσι λαβὼν, καταῤῥάκτης γε μὴν, καὶ ἴβις, καὶ πορφυρίων, προσθείην δ' ἂν ὅτι καὶ πελεκᾶνος, ἐπιμαίνονται τοῖς ἰχθύσι, καὶ τροφὴν ποιοῦνται τὸν ἐκείνων ὄλεθρον. Τοιοῦτοι δὲ πάντες, ὅσον ἧκεν εἰς τρόπους καὶ ἠθῶν ἀγριότητα, οἱ παρ' οὐδὲν ἡγούμενοι τὸ διολλύναι τινὰς, διά γε τὸ σφίσιν αὐτοῖς ἡδύ· οἳ τὸν τῆς φιλαλληλίας παρωσάμενοι νόμον, καὶ τοῖς τῆς ἀγάπης προσκεκρουκότες θεσμοῖς, καὶ τοῦτο εἰσάπαν ἀκούσειαν ἂν εἰκότως καὶ πρός γε ἡμῶν αὐτῶν· «Μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ζητεῖτε, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων· ἡ γὰρ ἀγάπη, φησὶ, τῷ πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται.» Παραιτεῖσθαι δὲ δεῖν ἔφη πάλιν γλαῦκα, καὶ ἐρωδιὸν, καὶ χαραδριὸν, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῶν, ἔποπα καὶ νυκτερίδα. Νυκτὸς δὲ οἶμαι φίλα ταυτὶ, καὶ χαίροντα μὲν τῷ σκότει, καὶ πτῆσιν ὡς ἡδυτάτην ἐν αὐτῷ ποιεῖσθαι μεμελετηκότα, κατεχθραίνοντα δὲ τὸ ἡλίου φῶς, καὶ τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ τι δρᾷν μὴ ἀνεχόμενα· εἶεν δ' ἂν οἱ τοιοίδε σαφῶς, οἱ τῶν φαύλων ἐργάται. Καὶ γάρ ἐστιν ἀληθὲς ὅπερ ἔφη Χριστὸς, ὅτι «Πᾶς ὁ φαῦλα πράσσων μισεῖ τὸ φῶς, καὶ οὐκ ἔρχεται εἰς τὸ φῶς, ἵνα μὴ ἐλεγχθῇ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ· ὁ δὲ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸ φῶς, ἵνα φανερωθῇ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἐν Θεῷ ἐστιν εἰργασμένα.» Ἀκάθαρτα δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑρπετὰ τῶν πετεινῶν, «ἃ πορεύεται,» φησὶν, «ἐπὶ τεσσάρων,» οἷον φέρε εἰπεῖν τὰ μυιῶν, καὶ εἴ τι τούτοις ἀγχοῦ. Μυρία δὲ ὅσα ταυτὶ μικρὰ καὶ ἀπόπτυστα, καὶ τὴν εἰς τὸ ὑψοῦ πτῆσιν οὐκ ἔχοντα. Τίς οὖν ἄρα ἐστὶ λόγος τοῦ καὶ ἐπ' αὐτὰ τὸν νόμον ἐλθεῖν, περιαθρεῖν ἀναγκαῖον. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ὅτε τῶν κτηνῶν ἐποιεῖτο μνήμην, τὴν κάμηλον ὀνομάσας, προσετίθει τὸν λαγωὸν, ἐν ἴσῳ που πάντως ἀκαθάρτους ἀποφαίνων τοὺς ἐπὶ φαυλότητι διαβεβλημένους, κἂν εἰ μέγας τις εἴη καὶ μικρὸς (προσωποληψία γὰρ οὐκ ἔστι παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον)· οὕτω κἀνθάδε διαμέμνηται μὲν ἀετοῦ, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν ὀνομάσας τὸν βασιλεύτατον, κάτεισι δὲ πάλιν καὶ ἐπ' αὐτὸ τὸ βραχὺ τῶν πτεροφορεῖν εἰωθότων, ἐν ἴσῳ τιθεὶς μικρόν τε καὶ μέγαν, εἰ τῶν ἐκτόπων εἴη δημιουργὸς, καὶ τὸ διαβεβλῆσθαι δεῖν, ἀνεξίτητον ἔχοι. Ὑπεξάγει γε μὴν τοῦ τοιούτου γέ
pass_a_gloss: [continuing] ...sharp toward wickedness, and having within themselves the baseness of their characters not apparent to the many. And there always grows beside those who have been sick with the accursed arrogance the wish to overreach whomever they may perhaps be able, and to besiege them by many-turning inventions of evil-doing, and so to plunder, and this insatiably. For this reason it joins on at once, saying: 'And ostrich and gull.' For these, I think, are most insatiable, and always collect what falls in their way. Then it says that: 'And hawk and the ones like it, and night raven, and plunging bird, and ibis, and purple gallinule, and pelican, and swan.' And these too would depict in themselves those who plot cruelly and savagely against others, and fasten on without restraint on whomever they may perhaps be able, so as not to refuse to bring on some even the danger and fear for life. For the hawk leaps down terribly on every weaker bird, and rushes against sparrows, and destroys them having taken them; and the plunging bird, and ibis, and purple gallinule, and I would add that the pelican also, rage against the fish, and make the destruction of those their food. And such are all, so far as it comes to ways and the savagery of characters, those who count as nothing the destroying of some for what is pleasant to themselves; who, having thrust aside the law of loving one another, and having struck against the ordinances of love, would fittingly hear this altogether even from us ourselves: 'Do not seek your own things, but also those of others; for love,' it says, 'works no evil to the neighbor.' And again it said one must refuse owl, and heron, and plover, and the ones like them, hoopoe and bat. And these, I think, are friends of night, and rejoice in the darkness, and have practiced to make their flight in it as most sweet, but they hate the light of the sun, and do not endure to do anything in it; and such would clearly be the workers of base things. For true indeed is what Christ said, that 'Everyone doing base things hates the light, and does not come into the light, so that his works may not be exposed; but the one doing the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been worked in God.' And unclean also are the creeping things of the birds, 'which go,' it says, 'upon four,' such as, let us say, the kinds of flies, and anything near to these. And countless are these small and spit-worthy things, and not having the flight toward the height. What then is the reason for the law coming even to these, it is necessary to look around at. For just as, when it made mention of the beasts, having named the camel, it added the hare, showing altogether equally unclean those accused for baseness, even if one should be great and small (for there is no respect of persons with God, according to what is written); so here also it makes mention of the eagle, naming the most kingly of the birds, and comes down again even to the very small of those accustomed to bear wings, setting equally both small and great, if he should be a craftsman of outrageous things, and should have the need of being accused inescapable. Yet it leads out from such a ki[nd — next section].
pass_b_english: Cyril: …in wickedness are in some way dark and not plain to all, and they keep the baseness of their character hidden within themselves, out of sight of the many. In those who are sick with the accursed disease of arrogance there always grows up beside it the wish to take advantage of whomever they can, to besiege them with wicked devices of every kind, and so to plunder them, and that insatiably. That is why it adds at once: ‘And the ostrich and the gull’ (Leviticus 11:16). For these, I think, are most insatiable, always gathering up whatever comes their way. Then it says: ‘And the hawk and its kind, the night raven, the cormorant, the ibis, the purple gallinule, the pelican and the swan’ (Leviticus 11:16–18). These too would portray in themselves those who plot cruelly and savagely against others and fasten without restraint on whomever they can, so that they do not shrink even from putting some in danger and fear for their very lives. For the hawk swoops fiercely on every weaker bird; it darts at sparrows, and when it catches them it kills them. The cormorant, the ibis and the purple gallinule, and I would add the pelican too, fall furiously on the fish and make their destruction their food. Such, as far as conduct and savagery of character go, are all who count it as nothing to destroy others for the sake of their own pleasure. They have thrust aside the law of mutual love and offended against the ordinances of love, and it would be altogether fitting for them to hear this, even from us: ‘Do not seek your own interests, but also those of others (Philippians 2:4; 1 Corinthians 10:24); for love,’ it says, ‘does no wrong to a neighbor’ (Romans 13:10). Again, it said that one must refuse the owl, the heron, the plover and their kind, the hoopoe and the bat (Leviticus 11:16–19). These, I think, are lovers of the night. They delight in the darkness and are practiced at taking their flight in it as their sweetest pleasure, but they hate the light of the sun and cannot bear to do anything in it. Such birds would plainly stand for those who work evil. For what Christ said is true: ‘Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been done in God’ (John 3:20–21). The winged creeping things too are unclean, those ‘which go,’ it says, ‘on all fours’ (Leviticus 11:20): for example, the various kinds of flies and anything akin to them. These are countless, small and loathsome, and they cannot fly high. We must therefore look closely at the reason why the law came down even to these. For just as, when it made mention of the beasts, it named the camel and then added the hare (Leviticus 11:4–6), declaring all those charged with wickedness equally unclean, whether one were great or small — for, as it is written, there is no partiality with God (Romans 2:11) — so here too it calls to mind the eagle, naming the most kingly of birds, but then comes down again to the very smallest of winged creatures, putting small and great on an equal footing if one is a worker of outrageous deeds, and so cannot escape the condemnation that is his due. Yet it does set apart from this kind…

Pass A rewritten 2026-10-23 as a plain English sense gloss of the Greek: the reviewed gloss interleaved Greek phrases with English, and once the Greek tags moved into lemmas[] too little English was left. Meaning unchanged; Pass B not touched.

Whole section is one continuing turn of Cyril that begins mid-word (δρι|μεῖς), so it carries the ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label. The old English placed John 3:20 beside ‘ostrich and gull’ and 1 Corinthians 10:24 beside the hawk list; both are corrected (Leviticus 11:16; 11:16–18). ‘Do not seek your own interests, but also those of others’ blends 1 Corinthians 10:24 (μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ζητείτω) with the wording of Philippians 2:4 (ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων); both are cited. ‘Love does no wrong to a neighbour’ is Romans 13:10. The camel and hare refer back to Cyril’s earlier treatment of the four-footed beasts (Leviticus 11:4–6; λαγωός is Cyril’s word for the animal of 11:6, which the LXX calls δασύπους). ‘No partiality with God’ is Romans 2:11 (compare Acts 10:34). Source has καταθρῶσκε· (OCR punctuation slip) read as καταθρῴσκει; καταῤῥάκτης here and καταράκτης in section 23 are the same bird. στρουθός (Leviticus 11:16) is kept as ‘ostrich’ for consistency with section 23, though Cyril may have understood a small greedy bird; στρουθία, the hawk’s prey, are ‘sparrows’. τὰ μυιῶν is taken as flies (μυῖα). The section ends mid-word (γέ|νους); the object (locust and young locust) follows in section 25. κτηνῶν is ‘the beasts’ (no ‘four-footed’ in the Greek); the Greek parenthesis on Romans 2:11 is set off with dashes to avoid nested brackets.
added ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label; trailing ‘…’ at the mid-word break
checked Leviticus 11:16, 11:16–18, 11:16–19, 11:20, 11:4–6 (camel, hare) against LXX verse divisions; Philippians 2:4 + 1 Corinthians 10:24 blend, Romans 13:10, John 3:20–21, Romans 2:11 confirmed
